items.title: China announces measures to steady stock market
text: BEIJING, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- China will roll out a slew of measures to steady the stock market, including lowering the minimum margin requirement for leveraged stock purchases to generate incremental funds, the country's securities regulator said Sunday.

With approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing stock exchanges will lower the minimum margin ratio from 100 percent to 80 percent, effective from Nov. 30, according to the CSRC.
The adjustment is estimated to theoretically bring in nearly 400 billion yuan (about 59.58 billion U.S. dollars) in incremental funds.

Adjustments to the ratio are seen as one of the key tools for conducting counter-cyclical regulation on China's stock market. Previous downward adjustments in history have increased margin balances and trading activity, playing a notable role in supporting the market, experts said.

The Shanghai and Shenzhen stock exchanges also introduced a new batch of fee reduction measures, including waiving the participant business unit usage fee, according to the CSRC. The measures waiving listing fees for listed companies and bond transaction handling fees, which were already implemented earlier this year, will be extended for two years to 2028.
The Shenzhen Stock Exchange on the same day began soliciting public opinion on the market-making rules for stocks on the ChiNext board, China's Nasdaq-style board of growth enterprises.

The introduction of the market-maker system for the board is an important institutional arrangement to bolster market-support forces, strengthen market resilience and improve the quality of operations, according to the exchange.
The measures came after China's major stock indices moved lower in recent days, while U.S. stocks plunged on Friday, unsettling investors.

Earlier this month, China's central bank stepped up monetary policy support for the capital market, conducting the third operation of the Securities, Funds and Insurance companies Swap Facility to help financial institutions secure funding and boost their capacity to buy stocks, and reducing the interest rate of a relending facility for share buybacks and shareholding increases.  ■

items.title: China Focus: China's second homegrown large cruise ship begins maiden commercial voyage
text: A tourist interacts with a robot on Adora Flora City, China's second domestically built large cruise ship, on Nov. 22, 2026. Adora Flora City embarked on its maiden voyage on Sunday, marking a new step in the country's efforts to expand cruise tourism and boost consumption.(Xinhua)

GUANGZHOU, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- China's second domestically built large cruise ship, Adora Flora City, embarked on its maiden voyage on Sunday, marking a new step in the country's efforts to expand cruise tourism and boost consumption.
Carrying more than 3,800 passengers, the ship departed from Guangzhou in south China's Guangdong Province on a six-day, five-night journey to Hong Kong and Hue, Vietnam.
Measuring 341 meters in length and with a gross tonnage of 141,900, the vessel has 2,130 cabins and can accommodate up to 5,232 passengers.

Construction of Adora Flora City began in August 2022. Operated by Adora Cruises under China Tourism Group, the ship was delivered in Shanghai, east China, on Nov. 6 and embarked on its first trial voyage on Nov. 9.

Shi Dai, chairperson of China Tourism Group, said the company is using cruise operations to drive the development of integrated cultural tourism products and travel experiences, aiming to set a new benchmark for vacations at sea.

Adora Flora City is larger and features a more streamlined design than its sister ship, Adora Magic City, China's first domestically built large cruise ship. Adora Magic City began commercial operations in January 2024 and has since completed about 250 voyages.

Hu Zhenyu, deputy director of the Qianhai branch of the China Development Institute, said the entry into service of two domestically built large cruise ships marks a new phase for China's cruise industry.
The development will not only expand the range of high-quality marine tourism products but also create new drivers of consumption in coastal areas, Hu said.

In 2027, Adora Flora City is scheduled to undertake over 50 international voyages from its home port in Guangzhou, offering both short getaways and longer itineraries to destinations including Vietnam, Malaysia and Brunei.
The ship will also offer voyages with no scheduled port calls, allowing passengers to enjoy the cruise ship as a destination in itself.

The vessel departed from the Guangzhou Nansha International Cruise Home Port, one of China's largest integrated cruise port complexes. A duty-free store at the terminal also opened on Sunday, adding a fresh shopping option for cruise passengers.

Wu Qingsong, deputy director of Guangzhou's culture, radio, television and tourism bureau, said the maiden voyage presents an opportunity for the city to better integrate its cruise port, shipping industry and tourism resources.

Guo Jia, assistant vice president of product and guest experience at Adora Cruises, said the company plans to expand year-round operations across multiple home ports in east and north China, and the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area, offering passengers more high-quality cruise experiences.

items.title: News Analysis: As Chinese universities use AI detectors to screen theses, questions arise over accuracy
text: BEIJING, Nov. 22 (Xinhua) -- After five rounds of revisions, one student still had a thesis flagged as 30 percent AI-generated by an artificial intelligence (AI) detector. Such results have become a source of anxiety for many graduating students in China.

As AI detection tools become more widely used in thesis reviews, some universities have made the "AI rate" a formal requirement alongside conventional plagiarism checks. A paper that passes the plagiarism check can still be barred from thesis defense if its AI rate exceeds the permitted threshold.

But the reliability of this technology is increasingly in question. Some detection platforms have flagged passages from classic Chinese literary works, including Zhu Ziqing's "Moonlight over the Lotus Pond" and writings by Lu Xun, as more than 80 percent AI-generated.

These cases highlight a problem facing universities as they try to regulate generative AI: a single percentage says little about how much intellectual work a student has actually done. Four scholars in the fields of law, communication and education, speaking to Xinhua, said the AI rate should not serve as a decisive standard.

Commercial AI detectors use AI to identify AI-generated writing, said Zhang Linghan, head of the institute of AI law at China University of Political Science and Law. They analyze statistical features such as perplexity and burstiness, assuming that machine-generated prose is unusually fluent and standardized while human writing varies in rhythm. Given the probabilistic method, no tool is fully accurate, she said, and a percentage alone "cannot serve as reliable evidence of academic misconduct."

Wang Feng, dean of the School of Communication at East China Normal University, said AI detection differs fundamentally from plagiarism screening. Plagiarism checks compare papers against existing texts and identify sources of overlap. AI detectors, by contrast, rely on algorithmic rules rather than traceable source texts. Results can vary across platforms using different data and algorithms, and can even differ when the same paper is submitted to the same platform at different times, he said.
Classic works can be flagged because the stylistic conventions detectors treat as markers of AI writing largely derive from classic literature, Wang added.

Xiong Bingqi, head of the 21st Century Education Research Institute in Shenzhen, south China, noted that plagiarism checks, introduced in China more than 20 years ago, had never resolved questions of originality: students could evade them by rewording or rearranging borrowed text. AI detectors, he said, similarly cannot determine whether a paper is original or innovative.

The limits of detection matter because students may use AI to search academic literature, polish language, draft an outline or generate an entire paper -- activities with very different academic implications that current detection tools cannot distinguish.

Xinhua Asia-Pacific news summary at 1600 GMT, Nov. 21
text: PHNOM PENH -- Retail fuel prices in Cambodia fell again on Saturday following a decline in international fuel prices, according to the Ministry of Commerce.

Regular gasoline dropped 6.5 percent to 1.00 U.S. dollar per liter, down from 1.07 dollars 10 days ago. Diesel fell 6.9 percent to 1.21 dollars per liter, down from 1.30 dollars. (Cambodia-Fuel Prices)

BANGKOK -- Thailand hopes to strengthen cooperation with China in high-tech sectors, including electric vehicles (EVs), batteries, energy storage and optoelectronics, and jointly explore third-country markets, Thai Industry Minister Varawut Silpa-archa said.

Chinese investment in Thailand's high-tech industries has continued to grow in recent years, Varawut told Xinhua in an interview. He called for closer technological exchanges and talent development to strengthen local supply chains and support industrial upgrading. (Thailand-China-Cooperation, INTERVIEW)

SINGAPORE -- There is an explosion of cultural confidence in Asian societies in the 21st century, according to Singaporean scholar Kishore Mahbubani, who identifies Asia's rapid economic growth as a key factor behind this resurgence.

"The fact that many Asian societies have done so well in the last few decades means that people have more time and countries have more resources to devote to cultural growth and renaissance," said Mahbubani, a distinguished fellow at the Asia Research Institute of the National University of Singapore and a former permanent representative of Singapore to the United Nations, in an interview with Xinhua ahead of his trip to Beijing for the Orchid Awards. (Singapore-Orchid Awards-Kishore Mahbubani, INTERVIEW)

TOKYO -- Japanese civic groups on Friday submitted a petition bearing 47,000 signatures to the Defense Ministry, opposing Japan's acquisition of nuclear-powered submarines and calling on the government to abandon the plan.

The joint petition was launched by several civil society organizations, including the Citizens' Nuclear Information Center, and collected the signatures in about one month, according to the organizers. (Japan-Nuclear Submarine-Opposition)  ■

items.title: Xinhua world news summary at 1530 GMT, Nov. 21
text: WASHINGTON -- The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is probing a breach of its nationwide criminal information database, CNN reported Friday night, citing two people briefed on the matter.

The intrusion of the National Crime Information Center by apparent hackers is the second such breach in recent months, the report said, noting that the database "serves as a lifeline" between federal, state and local law enforcement. (US-FBI-Cyberattack)
NEW DELHI -- At least 11 people were killed and 181 others hospitalized in the past 48 hours after consuming spurious liquor in India's northeastern state of Manipur, officials said Friday.
The incident took place in the Chakpikarong area of Chandel district in Manipur. (India-Liquor Deaths)

TEHRAN -- Iran is willing to end the current state of "neither war nor peace" through negotiations with the United States, and its proposed two-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz remains on the table, Iranian Foreign Minister Seyed Abbas Araghchi has said.

In a recent interview with Iranian media, Araghchi said that Tehran seeks a lasting agreement through diplomacy that would safeguard its national interests and prevent another war, on condition that the United States clearly expresses its willingness to reach an agreement and takes necessary confidence-building measures. (Iran-US-Negotiation)

BAGHDAD -- Four people were killed and 35 others injured in a fire at the al-Hartha thermal power station in Iraq's southern Basra province on Saturday, according to a preliminary assessment by the Security Media Cell, affiliated with the Iraqi Joint Operations Command.

Most of the injured are residents of informal housing, with varying degrees of burns and smoke inhalation, and were taken for first aid and medical care, the cell said in a statement. (Iraq-Power Station-Fire)  ■

items.title: Zelensky says Ukraine sank Russian corvette off Libyan coast
text: KYIV -- Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Monday that Ukrainian forces sank Russian navy corvette Merkury off the coast of Libya.
In a post on X, Zelensky described the vessel as one of Russia's newest warships, commissioned in 2023, during the full-scale conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
He said the operation, which involved seven Ukrainian-made naval drones, also destroyed a Ka-27 combat helicopter and hit dry cargo vessel MV ANGARA used by Russia to transport weapons.
The Security Service of Ukraine conducted the mission in coordination with the country's Defense Forces, according to Zelensky.

items.title: Song-Dynasty Jiangnan comes alive at Shanghai's Jinshan Museum
text:
By ZHANG KUN | 
          chinadaily.com.cn |
          Updated: 2026-11-23 11:29

Opening on Saturday, the new exhibition at Jinshan Museum in Shanghai's suburban Jinshan district, Jiangnan in Song Paintings, is the latest stop on the national tour of A Comprehensive Collection of Ancient Chinese Paintings.

The project behind it, launched in 2005, has grown into a national undertaking spanning more than two decades. Three worldwide image-gathering campaigns brought together 12,405 Chinese paintings (sets) from 263 institutions at home and abroad; the results were published in 257 books across 68 volumes — the most extensive illustrated archive of its kind.
The Jinshan stop, the 103rd on the tour, brings together 306 exhibits (sets) and runs through Feb 21, 2027.

The Song Dynasty (960–1279) was a golden age for Chinese painting. Jinshan — on the north shore of Hangzhou Bay and part of Xiuzhou during the Song period — was a land of crisscrossing waterways and reclaimed fields, of fishing, salt-making and mulberry cultivation: the very world the painters recorded.

Dong Yuan's Xiaoxiang Landscape and Xia Gui's Pure and Remote View of Streams and Mountains capture the region's soft, expansive hills; Li Song's The Peddler packs roughly 300 wares onto a village peddler's load, while an anonymous Song-dynasty Sericulture and Weaving scroll supplies the bustling human detail.
The exhibition opens with an immersive light-and-shadow prologue featuring 101 Song paintings, then unfolds across two halls and four sections.

items.title: Free noodles stir debate in Nanjing
text: A free vegetarian noodle shop in Nanjing, Jiangsu province, available to the elderly and gig workers, has sparked debate over individual charity and its impact on nearby businesses, with some restaurants reporting a loss of customers and others considering moving out.
The topic of the Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop drew at least 12 million views on Sina Weibo, a Chinese social media platform, as of Sunday.
The Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop, which opened its doors in October, serves vegetarian noodles free of charge to those in need, the Yangtse Evening Post reported in early November.
From the onset, the shop permitted everyone, with no restrictions on age or income, with the elderly and those working in the informal sector making up a large part of their customer base.
A customer surnamed Pan, who is job-hunting and has no fixed address, visited the shop twice, saying the noodles brought him immediate relief.

However, since Nov 14, after complaints from neighboring businesses, free meals are now only available to people aged 60 and above, people with disabilities, sanitation workers, couriers and food-delivery riders, the Yangtse Evening Post reported.
The owner, surnamed Zhang, told local media that he wanted to do some good with the shop. The shop's two outlets together serve about 3,000 bowls a day, Zhang said.
For nearby noodle restaurants, however, the free meals have affected business.

Huang Haoming, dean of the Hainan-based Asia Academy of Philanthropy, said individual charitable acts are not prohibited under China's Charity Law, although he acknowledged that free services could affect businesses depending on the circumstances.

Beijing News reported that a noodle shop about 100 meters from one of the outlets saw its daily turnover fall by about 200 yuan ($30) to 300 yuan after the Zero-Yuan Noodle Shop opened. Its owner, whose lease expires in March, plans to relocate, citing the free shop's presence nearby.

Another noodle shop about 800 meters away reported being less affected. Its owner said the free shop mainly attracted customers who would normally buy low-priced noodles, as well as elderly people who had time to wait in line.
Even so, the owner said he plans to relocate when his lease expires, as nearby noodle shops may lower their prices to survive, drawing them into a price war.
In contrast, another nearby noodle shop owner said turnover was still rising, crediting a stable base of regular patrons.

Zhang told the Yangtse Evening Post that the shop's single-item menu set it apart from nearby restaurants, which cater to a wider range of tastes and budgets. He said his shops could not start charging customers because the name had already ruled out that possibility. He added that no profit model had been designed so far.
Huang said helping people in need, including seniors who have no one at home to cook for them, was "definitely a charitable act".
"No law says that his charitable act is wrong, nor does the law prohibit him from doing it," he said.
"Doing charity is a citizen's right. It is something that should be encouraged, and the central government does encourage it."
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: From Yijing to Taoism, an enduring search for life's deeper meaning
text: In the autumn of 1969, 27-year-old Guy Alitto arrived in Taipei to continue his study of Chinese. He immediately noticed a cultural difference.

"I was overwhelmed by the way people would respond when you asked them for the location of a place. In the West, they would always give you the address, which is something absolute. But the Chinese would only describe it in relation to something else," recalls Alitto, an acclaimed China scholar and visiting professor at Beijing Language and Culture University.

"The more I thought about it, and the more I learned, I could see the fundamental difference was that Chinese thought was always relational, whereas there's almost nothing like that in Western thinking."

Alitto often recounted this story to his students at the University of Chicago, hoping to help them "appreciate how life could make sense to someone without the assumptions and values that the students carried around". The central ideas of those lectures have now found their way into his book The Uniqueness of Chinese Civilization in World History. In tracing the roots of relational thinking, Alitto turns to the Yijing, or Book of Changes, an ancient Chinese classic that he sees as the distillation of collective wisdom accumulated over several centuries leading up to the early Zhou period, around the 11th century BC.

At the heart of the Yijing is the interplay of yin and yang, opposing yet interdependent forces that define, complement and give rise to one another. Neither exists in isolation; each acquires meaning through its relationship with the other. Rather than viewing the world as a collection of fixed, self-contained entities, the Yijing presents it as an interconnected process of continual change. Its vision of the relationship between Heaven, Earth and humanity places human existence within a larger cosmic order, in which the meaning of things is shaped not only by their inherent qualities, but also by their relationships with the world around them.

Yet Alitto is equally struck by another feature of the Yijing: its reliance on symbols and images to convey meaning. Its 64 hexagrams, formed by different arrangements of broken and unbroken lines representing yin and yang, express a wide range of relationships and changing circumstances through a remarkably simple visual system. The text thus suggests that understanding the nature of things requires more than simply naming or describing them; it calls for an appreciation of the underlying patterns.

"Written words and even speech itself are static. We have to have an agreement about what my words mean before I say something to you. And that makes for a static relationship," Alitto says. "What the Yijing is trying to capture is the endless flow of things — a reality that changes every nanosecond."

This concern with the limits of language also has echoes in ancient Greek philosophy. Heraclitus saw the world as being in perpetual flux, yet shaped by an order that gives coherence to change; Plato questioned how stable knowledge could be attained in a world of constant change, while Aristotle distinguished words from the realities they represent.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: From fading mining town to Xinjiang ski destination
text: When 13-year-old Qadir Hali arrived in Koktokay in the Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region in 1942, he could scarcely have imagined that the mining town would one day become a destination for skiers from across China and beyond.
More than eight decades later, his son Kumash Qadir, now 63, has witnessed that transformation firsthand.

Once a major mining center, Koktokay, in Xinjiang's Altay prefecture, is now home to one of China's earliest-opening ski resorts. Since launching its 2026-27 season on Oct 20, the resort has welcomed nearly 25,000 visitors, including more than 22,000 skiers, in the first two weeks.
Koktokay, meaning "green forest" in Kazakh, sits in the mineral-rich Altay Mountains. After mines were discovered in 1935, Koktokay earned a reputation as a major industrial center.
But declining reserves and changing market demand brought economic hardship from the mid-to-late 1980s. The town's population fell from a peak of 50,000 to 60,000 to just over 10,000.
Kumash, who was born in Koktokay, followed his father into the mining industry and worked there for 20 years. He recalled a thriving town where sporting events were regularly held.
In 1999, as the mining industry declined, he lost his job.

"As a local who grew up here, I felt quite lonely at the time and had little certainty about the future. Some people urged me to move away, but I had grown up here and felt attached to my hometown, so I wanted to stay," he said.
To make a living, Kumash bought a car and began driving passengers between Koktokay and Urumqi, the regional capital. "Later the ski resort was built, and things slowly began to change," he recalled.
The Koktokay International Ski Resort opened in 2020, providing Kumash with a new job on its operations team.

His working day begins before dawn, when he drives his pickup truck to deliver safety nets to the slopes and anti-slip mats to the ski hall. In his spare time, he even helps care for a husky left with him by a skier.

"Now I have a job, and the basics of life are taken care of," he said. "In the past, herders had little to do in winter, and the villages and town were quiet. Now there is winter work. Some people work at the resort, some serve tourists, and some rent out their houses for extra income."
The tourism boom has also created opportunities for younger residents.
Ardak Salinbek, 28, works at a ski equipment shop at an altitude of 2,200 meters, serving nearly 100 customers a day in winter.

Born in Kairti Village, 15 kilometers from the resort, to a herder father and a farmer mother, she initially worked at a township hospital after graduating from medical school, earning less than 3,000 yuan ($425) a month.
"The pay wasn't high, and the work was rather dull. I felt the ski-gear business suited me better. I get to meet friends from all over the country and learn something new every day," she said.

Her parents initially questioned the career change but were convinced when she brought home her first monthly paycheck of 16,000 yuan. "As skiing in Koktokay became better known across the country, my parents realized it was a new opportunity for young people. They told me to 'go for it'," Salinbek recalled.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: COP31 ends without agreement on climate deal
text: The 31st session of the Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, or COP31, failed to reach consensus on the Antalya Pact on Sunday in Antalya, Turkiye.

After more than two weeks of negotiations that spilled two days into overtime, COP31 President Murat Kurum said at the closing plenary that he could see there was no agreement, confirmed he would not advance any new text, and later left the stage in the midst of speeches being delivered by country representatives.
"There is nothing to do, we did all that we could. Since there are 196 countries, they will make the decision and we will respect their ‌decision," he said.
The last time UN climate talks failed to get a deal adopted by all was in Copenhagen in 2009.

While a blow to efforts to ratchet up international action, the failure to agree on a political declaration in Antalya does not erase the obligations agreed upon by previous summits or remove the technical and legal ‌frameworks governing multilateral action against climate change.

Many delegates from developing countries arrived in Antalya hoping that COP31 would deliver stronger support for mitigation and adaptation. However, as the negotiations dragged on, those hopes increasingly gave way to frustration.
The mood was already visible at Friday night's plenary session, which began after 9 pm, more than an hour late. Shortly after the session opened, a protester interrupted Kurum.

Standing on a chair with a red noose around his neck and wearing a shirt that read "You are killing the future", the protester shouted: "There's no money. The Global South cannot wait," and "You are doing nothing, nothing at all."

The protester was escorted from the hall by security officers. The scene reflected the deep divisions among the participating countries over fossil fuels, climate finance and the direction of global energy transition.
Some NGOs warned that the conference was at risk of becoming one of the most disappointing COPs in recent years.

In an open letter to Kurum and Chris Bowen, COP31 president of negotiations, dozens of nongovernmental organizations around the world said: "The Global South is being abandoned." They accused developed countries of blocking progress and coming to the conference without new financial commitments.
"Without finance, communities on every front line will be sacrificed," they said.

Finance remained one of the most difficult issues. An earlier draft included language on tripling adaptation finance to at least $120 billion a year by 2035. But the second draft removed the explicit target, while the last proposal failed to provide a clear baseline or detailed delivery pathway for adaptation finance.
Developing countries had demanded greater clarity on how much money would be provided, by whom and on what terms.

The last draft also showed how the presidency sought to avoid a direct confrontation over fossil fuels. It retained a proposal to raise electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35 percent by 2035.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019305/Chinese Archaeologists Announce Findings From Four Key Sites
text: Chinese archaeologists have announced discoveries from four sites across the country, including Paleolithic campsite ruins and greater details of an aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture.

The findings, announced at a Wednesday conference held by China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration, come from four years of work at four sites along the Yangtze River. They include Taohuahe in the southwestern Sichuan province; Fanshan in Hangzhou, capital of the eastern Zhejiang province; Lingtoushang in the eastern Jiangxi province; and Laohudun in the central Hubei province.
The discoveries were presented by Archaeology China, a government program launched in 2018 to fund long-term excavations investigating the origins of farming and civilization.

Taohuahe, discovered in 2022, has yielded over 13,000 Paleolithic-age stone artifacts, including large stone choppers, and 179 animal fossils dating from 300,000 to 50,000 years ago, researchers at the conference announced. Excavations have also revealed stone-working and storage areas, cobblestone surfaces, and a semicircular refuse pit.
Wang Youping, an archaeologist at Peking University, told domestic media that, unlike in other archaeological digs in southern China, numerous animal bones have been recovered at Taohuahe.

“Southern China’s acidic soil usually destroys bone,” Wang said. “Researchers had assumed that people in the lush south relied mainly on plants. The (presence of animal) bones suggests that meat was equally important to their work, daily lives, and evolution.”

The second site discussed at the meeting, Fanshan, was discovered 40 years ago and is the highest-ranking aristocratic cemetery of the Neolithic Liangzhu culture ever found, researchers said. The Liangzhu culture, located in northern present-day Hangzhou, flourished about 5,000 years ago. UNESCO added the ruins of its walled city and system of dams and reservoirs to its World Heritage List in 2019.

Excavations that began in 2024 indicate that a walled compound enclosed the site’s cemetery mound. At least three buildings stood at its center, including a large oval structure raised on stilts, likely used for ceremonies. The compound lies on a ridge that formed part of the surrounding area’s water system, leading researchers to hypothesize that the tombs, ritual spaces, and dams were planned as a single complex.

After last year’s discovery of a courtyard wall at the Fanshan site, archaeologists uncovered a group of three related buildings this year. Wang said the wall may have formed the cemetery’s outer boundary, while the buildings may have served as sacrificial halls. He added that the culture may already have had a mausoleum system.

Researchers also announced at the conference that they have discovered Neolithic and Shang dynasty (c.1600–1046 BC) settlements at a third site, Lingtoushang. The settlements contained evidence of smelting and large quantities of copper, shedding light on close cultural exchange and how the societies exploited and controlled metal resources.
[continua sulla fonte originale]

items.title: Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019307/Lost Ground: China’s Coffee Brands Break Starbucks and Nestlé’s Grip on Yunnan
text: For coffee growers in China’s southwestern Yunnan province, Starbucks and Nestlé used to be the only buyers in town. Every harvest season, their purchasing stations would have lines of loaded trucks stretching for days.

Plantation owner Zou Qingquan recalls once waiting a whole week to sell her beans to Nestlé. Back then, she says, the company revised its purchase price twice a week based on changes in the international commodity market, “so your beans were making or losing money as they sat there in the truck.”

Over the past five years, however, these two global giants have been losing their grip on the Yunnan coffee market. Rapid growth among domestic brands such as Seesaw, Manner, Luckin, and the Mixue Group, along with a shift toward specialty coffee, has opened new sales channels for farmers and pushed up prices.

According to the agricultural industry analysis platform Beedata, Nestlé and Starbucks paid an average of 48.09 yuan ($7.20) and 48.18 yuan per kilogram, respectively, for commercial-grade Yunnan green beans in the first quarter of 2026. For Luckin, it was 50.37 yuan.

But while growers’ incomes have risen, some warn that an increasingly indiscriminate buying frenzy, which in some cases is leading to the sale of unripe beans, risks disrupting established trade relationships and negatively affecting the quality and image of Yunnan coffee.

Ma Xiaojin, who manages two coffee-growing cooperatives in Yunnan’s Menglian Dai, Lahu and Va Autonomous County, used to regularly drive the 10 hours from his farm to the Starbucks Farmer Support Center, a training and purchasing facility in central Pu’er, a city arguably best known for its eponymous tea. There, he’d join the line of trucks and wait four or five days to have his beans graded, costing him at least 2,000 yuan in truck rental costs.

Starbucks has exacting quality standards and purchases beans only from growers certified under its Coffee and Farmer Equity (CAFE) Practices program, which in January included 3,400 farms in Yunnan. The American company is also known for paying more for high-quality beans than its Swiss competitor, Nestlé.

“You can’t just show up and expect Starbucks to take your beans,” says Hao Yi, who used to work for Starbucks in coffee production. “They don’t just check each batch; they monitor your quality over several consecutive years. That’s why, in the early days, getting your beans into Starbucks was a source of pride. It also brought your subsequent harvests to the attention of specialty coffee roasters.”

In 2017, Starbucks began selling selected Yunnan beans as part of its high-end Reserve line. For growers, making the cut was no easy feat. If their products passed a preliminary check, they had to provide three large samples from each sack for testing and agree to follow-up screenings.

Specialty beans from Zou’s estate were selected in 2021, with Starbucks offering 48 yuan per kilogram. At the time, her farm was selling to the open market for more than 60 yuan per kilogram. “We earned less, but working with a big brand was good publicity for us, so it was still a net gain,” she says. The following year, many new buyers approached Zou to purchase the same beans.

items.title: China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019298/China’s Cargo Drones Take Off With Two Successful Trials
text: China has successfully tested two large unmanned cargo aircraft: one with a 5-ton payload capacity and the other capable of flying 3,000 kilometers, laying the groundwork for future commercial and emergency transportation systems.

On Tuesday, the country announced that the Changying-8, a domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, had completed a test delivery. Three days prior, another domestically developed unmanned cargo aircraft, the W5000, also completed its maiden flight.

The milestones come as China’s drone market is expected to exceed 140 billion yuan ($19.6 billion) by the end of 2026, with the industrial drone segment alone projected to reach 84 billion yuan, up 12.5% from last year.

China began testing large cargo drones as early as 2017 and incorporated the concept of the “low-altitude economy” into government policy in 2021. The Civil Aviation Administration of China has also laid out a roadmap to establish an air transportation system for unmanned aircraft by 2035.
During its delivery test, the Changying-8, developed by China North Industries Group Corporation, released a cargo pallet at an altitude of 300 meters before returning to its base.

The aircraft, whose maiden flight took place in Zhengzhou, capital of the central Henan province, on March 31, has a maximum range of over 3,000 kilometers, measures 17 meters in length, has a 25-meter wingspan, and an 18-cubic-meter cargo compartment volume, domestic media reported.

In the event of extreme disasters such as earthquakes, floods, and mudslides destroying roads and bridges, the aircraft can be used to transport up to 3.5 metric tons of goods, equal to over 700 disaster-relief tents, the head of the Changying-8’s development team told state news agency Xinhua.
According to its engineers, future applications could include transportation of regional cargo, emergency supplies, and cold-chain deliveries, domestic media reported.
On Saturday, the W5000, an unmanned cargo aircraft developed by Chinese aviation company Air White Whale, also completed its maiden flight in northern China’s Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region.

The aircraft flew for about 30 minutes at an altitude of 1,000 meters, completing a series of test maneuvers before landing. The test focused on the aircraft’s flight stability and the coordinated operation of its propulsion, flight control, electronics, and ground-based monitoring and control systems.

With a maximum payload capacity of 5 metric tons, the W5000 is billed as one of the world’s largest unmanned cargo aircraft by payload capacity. Made of carbon fiber and weighing less than 6 metric tons, the aircraft measures over 22 meters in both length and wingspan and can fly at a cruising speed of 526 kilometers per hour, with a maximum range of 2,600 kilometers, domestic media reported.
Hu Zhendong, founder, chairman, and CEO of Air White Whale, said the W5000 could reduce logistics costs per ton-kilometer by more than 60% compared with comparable crewed cargo aircraft.
The W5000 is expected to begin commercial operation by the end of next year, according to domestic media.

items.title: Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019294/Why China’s Latest Blockbuster Game Had a Change of Heart
text: One of the wildest boss fights in China’s latest hack-and-slash blockbuster game begins with a calligraphy brush. Soul, the protagonist of Phantom Blade Zero, released late last month, dots the eyes of a lion-dance head, performing a traditional Chinese ritual believed to awaken the eponymous beast.

Cue the violence. Two performers animate the lion, lunging at Soul with blades spinning on its head and flames pouring from its mouth. The fight then spills onto elevated wooden poles, where Soul and the lion-dance master leap from perch to perch, trading blows to pounding Chinese drums and screaming electric guitar.
In the game its creator originally envisioned, Soul had just 66 lives to survive this fight and every other. Use them up, and hours of progress across the campaign would be gone for good.

The restriction was meant to mirror the game’s story: Soul has just 66 days to find a replacement for his damaged heart. But Beijing-based developer S-Game eventually abandoned the compulsory death limit, introducing three difficulty settings and making the original challenge optional.

S-Game founder Liang Qiwei called the compromise “one of the countless difficult decisions we made in developing Phantom Blade Zero.” His studio spent four years and a reported 300 million to 400 million yuan ($45 million to $60 million) creating a game it hoped would introduce wuxia — Chinese martial arts fantasy — to audiences around the world.

To bring its combat to life, S-Game recruited Hong Kong action star Donnie Yen, enlisted martial arts experts, and brought traditional performers into motion-capture studios. The finished game features more than 50 bosses and 55 weapons, each offering different ways to fight.

The scale of the undertaking drew inevitable comparisons with Black Myth: Wukong, China’s breakout global gaming hit of 2024. Chinese gamers even dubbed Phantom Blade Zero “the village’s second college student,” hoping the conditions for success would align twice.

So far, it has. Video game rating site IGN gave Phantom Blade Zero a 9 out of 10, praising its “memorable boss fights, compelling combat, and limitless swagger.” Its PC version scored 88 on review aggregator Metacritic, surpassing the 81 Black Myth: Wukong received.

Released on Oct. 29, with a standard edition priced at 268 yuan ($40) and a deluxe edition at 328 yuan, the game sold more than 4 million copies in its first 72 hours, topping Steam’s bestseller chart and generating an estimated 1 billion yuan in gross sales.

Unlike Wukong, which drew on the beloved Chinese classic “Journey to the West,” Phantom Blade Zero had to win over players with a far less familiar fictional universe, one Liang had spent two decades developing.

In 2006, while studying architecture at Beijing’s Tsinghua University, Liang began developing Rain Blood, an independent role-playing game inspired by Taiwanese wuxia novelist Gu Long. Built using software intended for amateur game developers, it introduced Soul, an assassin serving the Order, a secretive organization of martial artists.

items.title: China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
items.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019293/China Proposes Tougher Rules to Curb Skills Certification Fraud
text: China has proposed its first regulation on vocational skills certifications, cracking down on fraudulent credentials and tightening oversight of certification bodies.
The Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security released the draft regulation on Nov. 12, with public feedback open until Dec. 12. No date has been set for when the rules will take effect.

China now has more than 220 million skilled workers — including electricians, AI trainers, and elderly-care workers — accounting for about 30% of its workforce, according to the ministry. Vocational skills certificates can bring benefits such as cash subsidies, children’s school enrollment, and fast-tracked residency applications.
Fraudulent vocational skills certificates have proliferated online in recent years, prompting a nationwide crackdown on bogus credentials in 2022.

The proposed regulation would tighten oversight of certification bodies, barring them from making misleading claims or leaking exam questions. In addition, certificates can be issued only to candidates who pass the required assessments, rather than those who simply pay to obtain them.

The draft also outlines that organizations responsible for vocational qualification assessments would be barred from offering related training. Institutions that issue certificates without first registering with the government, as well as those that forge, alter, or trade certificates, may face suspension, confiscation of illegal earnings, and fines of 10,000 to 100,000 yuan ($1,500 to $15,000).

The rules also outline penalties for examiners who engage in misconduct, candidates who cheat, and officials who fail to perform their duties properly. Employers will be encouraged to use workers’ certified skill levels as a key factor in determining pay.

Previously, workers obtained vocational qualifications through government-organized exams. Starting in 2020, however, China phased out most government-issued vocational qualifications, shifting responsibility to registered and supervised third-party organizations. By the end of 2025, 32,000 such organizations were in operation nationwide.

Cheng Xiezhong, a law professor at the China University of Political Science and Law, told domestic media that the shift had “helped expand the pool of skilled workers” but had also led to uneven standards among certification bodies and a widespread increase in bogus certificates.

An investigation by domestic media this June found vocational certificates openly advertised on multiple Chinese e-commerce platforms. In one case, a reporter paid just 300 yuan for a mechanical equipment installer certificate showing passing scores on tests they had never taken.

Previous reports also found that some training providers issued course completion certificates rather than recognized vocational credentials. Others lured young jobseekers into “training loan” scams, persuading them to borrow thousands of yuan for courses.

items.title: China sets new record in deep oil well casing replacement in Xinjiang region
text: The Xinjiang Oilfield, a major oil production base in northwestern China, belonging to the China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) has announced that it has completed a deep underground casing replacement trial at a depth of 1,819 meters, setting a new domestic record and marking progress in technologies designed to repair aging oil wells and extend their service life, the China News Service reported Saturday.

The expanded field trial was recently completed at a Gobi Desert drilling site in the Luliang oilfield, with the operation successfully reconnecting 1,819 meters of casing and completing cementing work in the space between the casing and the surrounding wellbore.

The achievement extends the limits of a technique developed by the oilfield to tackle severe damage to underground well casings, which can otherwise make wells difficult to maintain and continue operating.

In an oil well, steel casing pipes are installed inside the drill hole to support the well walls and provide a stable passage for extracting oil or injecting water. Over years of operation, however, these pipes can corrode, become deformed or break, potentially restricting the well's internal passage and disrupting production.

At the Xinjiang Oilfield, located in the Junggar Basin in Northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, prolonged exposure to highly mineralized water and the gradual deformation of water-absorbing mudstone formations have contributed to increasingly serious casing damage, including large sections suffering leakage and broken pipes.

Conventional repair methods, such as plugging damaged sections, may only address the immediate leakage without removing the underlying damaged casing. Meanwhile, traditional casing replacement techniques used in shallower sections are not well suited to the complicated conditions encountered deeper underground.

To address the problem, researchers at the Xinjiang Oilfield's Oil Production Technology Research Institute developed a deep open-hole casing replacement technique in 2025. The approach involves removing damaged casing sections and installing replacement pipes, aiming to restore the wellbore to its original internal diameter rather than simply sealing the damaged areas.

An initial field trial was successfully conducted in October 2025 at Well 1424, operated by the Baikouquan Oil Production Plant. The operation replaced casings at a depth of 996 meters and accomplished 809 meters of open-hole casing milling, setting two domestic records at the time.
Building on the experience, the research team continued refining the technique in 2026, focusing on several challenges that had affected the efficiency and safety of deep underground operations.

These included difficulties in milling long unsupported sections of casing, the risk of tools becoming stuck when working along the edge of the casing, and the time-consuming process of cutting and retrieving damaged pipes at greater depths.

items.title: China unveils 34 new flagship smart factories, highlighting AI-driven transformation
text: China on Thursday unveiled 34 flagship smart factories across 20 provincial-level regions, expanding the initiative into more consumer-facing industries as the country steps up efforts to integrate artificial intelligence (AI) technology into manufacturing, boost productivity and accelerate the digital transformation of its industrial sector.

The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) and five other departments released the 2026 flagship smart factory cultivation list, which includes major manufacturers such as Xiaomi Auto. Pharmaceutical and apparel manufacturers were included for the first time, highlighting the initiative's widening industry coverage.

As the second batch of flagship smart factories, they have reported an average 34.4 percent increase in labor productivity and a 19.3 percent rise in production efficiency, while helping nearly 4,000 enterprises carry out digital and intelligent transformation in coordination.

Notably, industry coverage has further expanded compared with the previous batch. Beyond equipment manufacturing, steel, electronic information and other fields, pharmaceutical and apparel enterprises in the consumer goods sector were included for the first time, according to the list released by the MIIT.

The list includes smart factory projects from leading Chinese manufacturers across the vehicle, power equipment and shipbuilding sectors, including Xiaomi Auto, FAW-Volkswagen, Harbin Electric Machinery and Hudong-Zhonghua Shipbuilding.

The announcement by the six departments calls for supporting flagship smart factories in building high-quality industrial datasets, developing industrial AI agents, exploring advanced manufacturing models and establishing smart supply chains. The requirements highlight a broader shift in smart factory development, from equipment automation toward deeper integration of AI, industrial data and supply chain coordination.
The MIIT announced 15 candidate factories on November 24, 2025, so the latest batch brings the total number to 49.

Li Changan, a professor at the School of Public Administration at the University of International Business and Economics, told the Global Times on Thursday that the integration of AI with manufacturing is a major technological force driving the development of modern manufacturing.

The inclusion of pharmaceutical and apparel manufacturers in the latest list shows that AI technologies are expanding beyond a limited number of industries and becoming increasingly integrated into traditional manufacturing sectors, according to Li.

The expert further noted that the list not only reflects the progress of AI applications in manufacturing, but also serves as a demonstration and a model for the wider industry, encouraging more traditional manufacturers to accelerate technological upgrades and transformation. This trend is expected to further strengthen China's manufacturing capabilities, improve product quality and enhance the global competitiveness of its manufacturing sector.

items.title: China’s vehicle export trains hit 10,000 trip milestone amid surging overseas demand
text: China's dedicated freight trains carrying domestically manufactured vehicles for export have made a cumulative 10,000 trips, a milestone in the country's expanding automobile exports as growing overseas demand and improving international logistics networks support the industry's global expansion.

The milestone was reached on Thursday when a train carrying 203 Chinese-made new-energy vehicles (NEVs) departed from Zhengzhou International Land Port in Central China's Henan Province, CCTV News reported. The vehicles will travel by rail to Shanghai before being loaded onto a roll-on/roll-off vessel bound for Australia, a journey of more than 10,000 kilometers.

The accelerating rail services reflect robust overseas demand for Chinese-made vehicles. More than 2.035 million vehicles have been transported for export by rail so far this year, up 79 percent year-on-year, according to CCTV News.

The growth comes amid a broader expansion in China's automobile exports. The country exported 9.271 million vehicles in the first 10 months of 2026, up 65.1 percent year-on-year, according to data from the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers released on November 11.

NEV exports reached 4.612 million units during the period, rising 130 percent year-on-year. October alone saw exports of 1.066 million vehicles, marking the fifth consecutive month that shipments exceeded 1 million units.

China's expanding presence in overseas markets has provided further momentum. Industry data showed that Brazil, Belgium, the UK, Australia and Thailand were among the leading destinations for Chinese NEV exports in the first nine months, reflecting demand across Latin America, Europe and the Asia-Pacific region.
Improvements in cross-border logistics have strengthened the industry's export capacity.

To meet growing demand for vehicle exports, railway operators have expanded regular routes through land ports including Horgos, Manzhouli and Alashankou, while using the China-Laos Railway to reach Southeast Asian markets. Combined with expanding rail-sea intermodal services, these routes are strengthening international logistics links for Chinese automakers, a Chinese expert noted.

The expansion of transport capacity and more efficient rail-sea connections are helping Chinese automakers reach overseas customers, underscoring how manufacturing competitiveness and logistics infrastructure are supporting the industry's growing role in global markets, Zhang Xiang, a visiting professor in the engineering department of Zhengzhou-based Huanghe Science and Technology University, told the Global Times on Thursday.

Democrats split over who should lead China oversight
text: The House Select Committee on China may be coming to an end with Democrats taking over the House majority in January.
Rep. Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is poised to be the next Speaker of the House, is ultimately responsible for whether the committee continues or is disbanded.
He says discussions about its fate won’t happen in earnest until after Democrats choose their leadership team.
Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the likely incoming chair of the House Foreign Affairs panel, told The Hill that his committee is capable of taking over the select panel’s responsibilities.
“We have the ability to do it. We’re ready to do it. We’ll do it. But I’ll follow the leader,” he told The Hill.

Supporters of the select committee, formally known as the Select Committee on Strategic Competition between the United States and the Chinese Communist Party, say the panel established by the GOP House in 2023 is the best venue for bipartisan cooperation on confronting Beijing.

But Democrats on the Foreign Affairs Committee are itching to take the lead on investigations and legislation that the select committee has overseen. They are particularly interested in focusing on President Trump’s dealings with China, including the fallout from allegations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang — a close adviser to Trump — had a romantic relationship with a suspected Chinese spy and tech business partner.
Democrats are also probing whether the administration prized profits over national security and allowed China in the process to illegally access advanced U.S. technology.
“We’ve got great talent on our committee,” Meeks told The Hill. “First we’ve got to see what the next Speaker is going to say. Once he makes his decision then we’ll plan accordingly.”

The Foreign Affairs panel has two subcommittees focused on Asia: one on East Asia and the Pacific and one on South and Central Asia. Meeks said he’s likely to overhaul the panel’s subcommittees in the new Congress.
“All of those committees, I’ve got to decide what I’m going to do – those committees were set up by the Republicans. They might not be the same committees once I make my determination,” he said.
Rep. Brad Sherman (D-Calif.), a member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, sees that committee as “well-positioned to conduct oversight of the administration’s China policy.”

Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi (D-Ill.), a member of the Select Committee on China and its initial ranking member, told The Hill the panel is “absolutely” essential to combat escalating challenges from Beijing.

“Now, in the face of the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] relentlessly kind of promulgating aggression toward us, whether it’s technologically, militarily, or economically — as we just saw with Jensen Huang and Nvidia — I feel like we need to stand firm on a bipartisan basis, and bicameral basis in holding the CCP at bay,” he said.

Gold Deluge Keeps China’s $1 Trillion Trade Surplus in Check
text: China’s gold imports surged to a record $209 billion so far this year, in an unprecedented buying spree that followed a promise by top officials to make their country into the world’s marketplace instead of just its factory.

The shift began in January — the same month Vice Premier He Lifeng made that vow in front of a crowd at Davos — as the value and volume of bullion imports more than doubled from the month before. Non-monetary gold purchases continued climbing in the 10 months through October, reaching a historical high that’s equivalent to nearly 8% of overall imports in the period, the latest data showed Friday.
